summary:
Private same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is legal in the Central African Republic for both men and women. Criminal liability attaches only to public conduct.

Article 85 of the criminal code punishes public expression of love between persons of the same sex as an attack on public morals. The penalty is imprisonment of six months to two years or a fine of 150,000 to 600,000 CFA francs. The law treats this conduct more severely than other public moral offences.

Where one participant is a child, the adult faces imprisonment of two to five years or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs.

Legal gender recognition is not permitted in the Central African Republic. A trans visitor cannot change a gender marker and will be assessed against documents as issued.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in health, employment, education, or access to goods and services. A visitor refused care, service, or assistance has no statutory basis for a complaint, according to the United States State Department 2023 report.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition. Article 7 of the Constitution defines marriage as the union between one man and one woman and bans same-sex marriage. Public affection between same-sex partners falls within reach of the public morals provision.

Alternatives Centrafrique, founded in 2009 and registered in 2020, documented mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ people by law enforcement, including arrests based on false accusations of same-sex intercourse. The United States State Department reported that criminalisation of public same-sex activity had pushed the community underground.

Societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons was described as entrenched. Many citizens attributed homosexuality to undue outside influence. Other accounts described same-sex conduct as taboo, viewed as imported from outside the region and contrary to local values. The community conceals itself. Maintaining queer relationships was described as dangerous.

No transgender-specific criminal, documentary, screening, facilities, custody, or care rule was sourced beyond the absence of gender recognition. All other rules affecting a trans visitor are stated on an LGBTQ-collective basis.

Two narrow formal protections were sourced. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data treats sexual orientation as sensitive data, with Article 17 prohibiting any processing of sensitive data due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms. The Central African Republic signed the United Nations joint statement condemning violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Neither creates an enforceable remedy for refusal of service or police abuse.
tangentialFactors:
The Central African Republic received two Universal Periodic Review recommendations concerning non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and improving the situation of sexual minorities.

The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights summary of stakeholders submissions for the 45th session in January 2024 included sexual orientation and gender identity related recommendations.

Alternatives Centrafrique submitted reports for the third and fourth Universal Periodic Review cycles.
localsOnly:
Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military.

No law prohibits the use of psychological or medical practices as conversion therapy on LGBTQ people. Religious preaching of conversion was reported as rarely enacted because people keep LGBTQ identities hidden.

Residents face documented discrimination in education, healthcare, and employment linked to criminalisation of public same-sex affection and cultural stigma.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement under the public expression provision is unresolved. No reports of police arrests or detentions under these provisions were recorded in 2012.

Reports of violence against LGBTQ people are unresolved. Sources record no reports of such violence but state it is unclear whether this reflects an absence of incidents or failure to report.

Organisational presence is not fully resolved. The United States State Department 2023 report stated there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights, while other sources document Alternatives Centrafrique as active and registered since 2020.

Transgender-specific rules on airport or police screening, access to sex-segregated facilities, detention placement, and gender-affirming care were not sourced.

The United States State Department 2012 report documents general abuses by security forces but contains little LGBT-specific material and was not used for findings on trans visitors.
